{{Short description|Range of application for a quantifier or connective in a logical formula}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=June 2024}}
In [[logic]], the '''scope''' of a [[Quantifier (logic)|quantifier]] or [[Logical connective|connective]] is the shortest formula in which it occurs,<ref name="BostockIntermediate">{{Cite book |last=Bostock |first=David |title=Intermediate logic |date=1997 |publisher=Clarendon Press; Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-875141-0 |location=Oxford : New York |pages=8, 79}}</ref> determining the range in the [[Well-formed formula#Predicate logic|formula]] to which the quantifier or connective is applied.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Cook |first=Roy T. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JfaqBgAAQBAJ |title=Dictionary of Philosophical Logic |date=March 20, 2009 |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |isbn=978-0-7486-3197-1 |pages=99,180,254 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last1=Rich |first1=Elaine |url=https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~dnp/frege/quantifier-scope.html |title=Quantifier Scope |last2=Cline |first2=Alan Kaylor |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Makridis |first=Odysseus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DoBgEAAAQBAJ |title=Symbolic Logic |date=February 21, 2022 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-67396-3 |pages=93–95 |language=en}}</ref> The notions of a [[Free variables and bound variables|free variable and bound variable]] are defined in terms of whether that formula is ''within the scope'' of a quantifier,<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=January 21, 2017 |title=3.3.2: Quantifier Scope, Bound Variables, and Free Variables |url=https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Philosophy/A_Modern_Formal_Logic_Primer_(Teller)/03%3A_Volume_II-_Predicate_Logic/3.03%3A_More_about_Quantifiers/3.3.02%3A_Quantifier_Scope_Bound_Variables_and_Free_Variables |access-date=June 10, 2024 |website=Humanities LibreTexts |language=en}}</ref> and the notions of a {{glossary link|glossary=Glossary of logic|dominant connective}} and {{glossary link|glossary=Glossary of logic|subordinate connective}} are defined in terms of whether a connective includes another ''within its scope''.'''<ref name="LemmonLogic" />'''<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Gillon |first=Brendan S. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8MuIDwAAQBAJ |title=Natural Language Semantics: Formation and Valuation |date=March 12, 2019 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-03920-8 |pages=250–253 |language=en}}</ref>

== Connectives ==
{{Logical connectives sidebar}}
The scope of a logical connective occurring within a formula is the smallest [[well-formed formula]] that contains the connective in question.<ref name=":0" />'''<ref name="LemmonLogic">{{Cite book |last=Lemmon |first=Edward John |title=Beginning logic |date=1998 |publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC |isbn=978-0-412-38090-7 |location=Boca Raton, FL |pages=45–48}}</ref>'''<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Examples {{!}} Logic Notes - ANU |url=https://users.cecs.anu.edu.au/~jks/LogicNotes/connectives.html |access-date=June 10, 2024 |website=users.cecs.anu.edu.au}}</ref> The connective with the largest scope in a formula is called its ''dominant connective,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Suppes |first1=Patrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=38LCAgAAQBAJ |title=First Course in Mathematical Logic |last2=Hill |first2=Shirley |date=April 30, 2012 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-15094-9 |pages=23–26 |language=en}}</ref>''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kirk |first=Donna |url=https://openstax.org/books/contemporary-mathematics/pages/2-2-compound-statements |title=Contemporary Mathematics |date=March 22, 2023 |publisher=OpenStax |chapter=2.2. Compound Statements}}</ref> ''main connective'','''<ref name="LemmonLogic" />'''<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":4" /> ''main operator'',<ref name=":0" /> ''major connective'',<ref name=":2" /> or ''principal connective'';<ref name=":2" /> a connective within the scope of another connective is said to be ''subordinate'' to it.'''<ref name="LemmonLogic" />'''

For instance, in the formula <math>(\left( \left( P \rightarrow Q \right) \lor \lnot Q \right) \leftrightarrow \left( \lnot \lnot P \land Q \right))</math>, the dominant connective is ↔, and all other connectives are subordinate to it; the → is subordinate to the ∨, but not to the ∧; the first ¬ is also subordinate to the ∨, but not to the →; the second ¬ is subordinate to the ∧, but not to the ∨ or the →; and the third ¬ is subordinate to the second ¬, as well as to the ∧, but not to the ∨ or the →.'''<ref name="LemmonLogic" />''' If an [[Logical connective#Order of precedence|order of precedence]] is adopted for the connectives, viz., with ¬ applying first, then ∧ and ∨, then →, and finally ↔, this formula may be written in the less parenthesized form <math>\left ( P \rightarrow Q \right) \lor \lnot Q \leftrightarrow \lnot \lnot P \land Q
</math>, which some may find easier to read.'''<ref name="LemmonLogic" />'''

== Quantifiers ==
The scope of a quantifier is the part of a logical expression over which the quantifier exerts control.<ref name=":1" /> It is the shortest full sentence<ref name=":3" /> written right after the quantifier,<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /> often in parentheses;<ref name=":1" /> some authors<ref name=":6" /> describe this as including the variable written right after the universal or existential quantifier. In the formula {{math|∀''xP''}}, for example, {{math|''P''}}<ref name=":3" /> (or {{math|''xP''}})<ref name=":6">{{cite book |last1=Bell |first1=John L. |title=A Course in Mathematical Logic |last2=Machover |first2=Moshé |date=April 15, 2007 |publisher=Elsevier Science Ltd |isbn=978-0-7204-2844-5 |page=[https://archive.org/details/courseinmathemat0000bell/page/17 17] |chapter=Chapter 1. Beginning mathematical logic |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/courseinmathemat0000bell/page/17 |authorlink1=John Lane Bell |authorlink2=Moshé Machover}}</ref> is the scope of the quantifier {{math|∀''x''}}<ref name=":3" /> (or {{math|∀}}).<ref name=":6" />

This gives rise to the following definitions:{{refn|group=lower-alpha|These definitions follow the common practice of using [[Greek alphabet|Greek letters]] as [[metalogic]]al symbols which may stand for symbols in a formal language for [[Propositional calculus|propositional]] or [[First-order logic|predicate logic]]. In particular, <math>\phi</math> and <math>\psi</math> are used to stand for any [[Well-formed formula|formulae]] whatsoever, whereas <math>\xi</math> and <math>\zeta</math> are used to stand for [[propositional variable]]s.<ref name="BostockIntermediate" />}}
* An occurrence of a quantifier <math>\forall</math> or <math>\exists</math>, immediately followed by an occurrence of the variable <math>\xi</math>, as in <math>\forall \xi</math> or <math>\exists \xi</math>, is said to be <math>\xi</math>-binding.<ref name="BostockIntermediate" /><ref name=":3" />
* An occurrence of a variable <math>\xi</math> in a formula <math>\phi</math> is ''free in'' <math>\phi</math> if, and only if, it is not in the scope of any <math>\xi</math>-binding quantifier in <math>\phi</math>; otherwise it is ''bound in'' <math>\phi</math>.<ref name="BostockIntermediate" /><ref name=":3" />
* A ''closed'' formula is one in which no variable occurs free; a formula which is not closed is ''[[Open formula|open]]''.<ref name=":7">{{Citation |last=Uzquiano |first=Gabriel |title=Quantifiers and Quantification |date=2022 |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2022/entries/quantification/ |access-date=June 10, 2024 |edition=Winter 2022 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}}</ref><ref name="BostockIntermediate" />
* An occurrence of a quantifier <math>\forall \xi</math> or <math>\exists \xi</math> is ''vacuous'' if, and only if, its scope is <math>\forall \xi \psi</math> or <math>\exists \xi \psi</math>, and the variable <math>\xi</math> does not occur free in <math>\psi</math>.<ref name="BostockIntermediate" />
* A variable <math>\zeta</math> is ''free for'' a variable <math>\xi</math> if, and only if, no free occurrences of <math>\xi</math> lie within the scope of a quantification on <math>\zeta</math>.<ref name=":7" />
* A quantifier whose scope contains another quantifier is said to have ''wider scope'' than the second, which, in turn, is said to have ''narrower scope'' than the first.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Allen |first=Colin |title=Logic primer |last2=Hand |first2=Michael |date=2001 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-51126-1 |edition=2nd |location=Cambridge, Mass |pages=66}}</ref>
